newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia miners are going for gold in Ghana.
newsitem.headline: Australia miners are going for gold in Ghana.

text.p: Ghana is emerging as a destination for Australian gold mining companies looking to expand overseas, mine executives said on Wednesday.

Sometimes frustrated by what they see as growing anti-mining sentiment in Australia, or, more often, seeing opportunities in the West African nation that may no longer exist at home, Australian miners are lifting their presence in Ghana.
"In Australia, you don't know who owns the bloody ground because of native title," said David Cairns, director of development for Perth-based Resolute Ltd.
Resolute is developing the Obotan gold deposit located 215 km northwest of the Ghanian capital Accra, estimated to contain proven and probable reserves of over 900,000 ounces of gold.

In comments made during and after a seminar on Ghana's mining industry on Wednesday sponsored by stockbroker Hartley Poynton Ltd, mining executives portrayed a developing nation anxious to open its borders to foreign mining companies.

"Ghana is one gold belt as far as I'm concerned," said Alex Black, executive chairman of African Gold Resources Ltd, which is exploring over more than 1,000 km of ground in Ghana and hopes to list on the Australian Stock Exchange this year.
Ghana, the original Gold Coast, currently ranks eleventh in the world in gold production, well behind Australia, ranked third.
Gold mining is dominated by the Obusai lode, operated by Ashanti Goldfields Co Ltd, which produces in excess of 900,000 ounces of gold a year.
But more mines are planned as new technologies, much of which was developed in the remote eastern goldfields of Western Australia, are now being applied to the rough terrain of Ghana.
Gold production in Ghana has increased 500 percent in the last 10 years.
The former Ghana high commissioner to Australia, Kevin Dzang, said encouraging Australians to mine in his country was once unthinkable given Australia's own vast reserves.
Besides, he said, Ghanaians were "never in a hurry to take their gifts out of the ground... saving them for their grandchildren."
But as the political turmoil that rocked the former British colony in previous decades subsided and ownership of gold was decriminalised, things started to change, Dzang said.
Now, Dzang said, "Sovereign interference in investment is very minimal."
In 1992, after 11 years of military rule, administration of Ghana was handed over to an elected government.

"In the early 1990s it was only those with the courage and know-how who got into Ghana," said Colin Roberts, operations manager for West Africa from Stanley Mining Services Ltd, which operates 18 exploration drill rigs in Ghana.
Bureaucracy is still part of every day life in Ghana, which can slow approval of foreign projects, although unlike in Australia, few uncertainties exist in the process.
Ghana requires a flat 10 percent stake in all projects and provides a two-year tax holiday to miners, followed by a 35 percent company rate.

In Australia's most prolific gold-producing state, Western Australia, native title claims exist on most deposits and miners are facing the possibility of a first-time ever royalty levy that threatens to make some mines uneconomical.
"In Ghana, the government's 10 percent is the royalty," said Resolute's Cairns.
But as more foreign gold miners stake out parts of Ghana, the pickings may be diminishing and becoming more expensive.

"A lot of Ghana already is pegged out," said Reg Gillard, executive chairman of Leo Shield Exploration NL, an Australian company which will spend up to A$5 million on exploration in the country this year.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
